We want to thank you for your feedback on our previous book, «Qubic. The Long Version». It made this book better before this one was even started.

Our previous book — «Qubic. The Long Version» — assembled the Qubic universe into a single fresco: the mechanism, the details, the functions of one large whole. This book is different. It is about a man. About a twenty-five-year line stretched from an article in a Minsk computer newspaper to an event that happened in the summer of 2026 on the screens of hundreds of home computers around the world. «The Long Version» answered the question ”how does this work.” This book answers the questions ”who is building it, and why”, and at its end you will find answers to riddles you may have long stopped hoping to solve. We’ll say no more: the hero of this book does not like it when endings are given away ahead of time. This book is distributed absolutely freely. blocks.text: The time machine exists.

Yes, that is hard to believe. The science fiction writers are largely to blame: they decided how the machine was supposed to look and how it was supposed to work — a chair, levers, dates blinking on a counter, or even a DeLorean. Which is exactly why everyone who goes looking for a time machine goes looking for a chair with levers. Hard to blame them. The human mind finds the very concept of ”time” catastrophically difficult to grasp. Time.
Close your eyes for a minute and keep reading with them closed. Feel the full depth and inevitability of this phenomenon.

That’s the whole catch: time is one of the few things we are stuck inside of with no way out, and which no one has ever seen. We have no organ for time. There are eyes for light, skin for warmth, a cochlea in the ear for sound. For time — nothing. All we have is memory of what no longer is, and expectation of what is not yet. Out of these two ”nots” the brain glues together the thing we call a life.

Test it on yourself. What is ”soon”? How far is it from ”a long time”? To a child, a ten-hour flight is an entire life, it has to be lived through, you could manage to grow old inside it. To an adult, the same flight is an annoying pause between two smoke breaks. This is plain arithmetic: at five years old, one year is a fifth of your whole life, an enormous slab of existence; at fifty, it is one fiftieth — a thin slice.

The French philosopher Paul Janet noticed this back in 1877: time does not flow evenly, it accelerates as you live. Right now it is moving faster for you than it ever has before. Tomorrow it will move faster still. And so on, always.

The only honest word in this whole madness is ”now.” And even that one blurs under close inspection. The psychologist William James, the first to examine ”now” under a magnifying glass, wrote in 1890:

”…the practically cognized present is no knife-edge, but a saddle-back, with a certain breadth of its own on which we sit perched, and from which we look in two directions into time.” Even ”now” is not a point. We sit astride something that has its own width, and no one can say where it begins and where it ends.

Then physics delivered a blow that still staggers today. In March 1955, a month before his own death, Albert Einstein wrote in a letter to the family of his late friend Michele Besso: ”People like us, who believe in physics, know that the distinction between past, present and future is only a stubbornly persistent illusion.”

This is the author of relativity writing, to the family of a friend who has just died — that ”earlier” and ”later” do not mean what we think they mean. A dying physicist consoling the grieving not with faith. With equations.

And the equations are on his side. In 1967 the physicists John Wheeler and Bryce DeWitt derived an equation that claims to describe the quantum state of the entire universe at once. They wrote the equation down. They looked at it. And they found the thing physics prefers to mention in a whisper: there is no time variable in it. In the master equation of the universe — if it is correct — time takes no part. Science does not like this subject; like you a minute ago, it can’t manage to read with its eyes closed.
This book is written about a man who learned to operate time, and about what he is building. His name is the key spoiler of this book’s plot: Come-from-Beyond. The one who came from beyond.
The Broken Question

In 1781 Immanuel Kant ran a strange experiment. He took the question ”does the world have a beginning in time?”, and honestly proved both answers. First: it does, because otherwise an infinity would have had to pass before any given moment, and an infinity cannot be passed. Second: it does not, because otherwise empty time would gape before the beginning, and in empty time there is nothing for anything to begin from. Two proofs. Both impeccable. Both incompatible.

From this Kant drew a conclusion the world still hasn’t fully digested: if reason proves ”yes” and ”no” with equal rigor, it is not the world that is broken. It is the question. Time is not a property of the universe but a lens through which a human looks at it. Asking ”what was there before time began” is like asking what lies north of the North Pole. The words form a sentence; the sentence does not form a meaning.
The River with No Source
A century and a half later, that same broken question broke the career of Britain’s finest astrophysicist.

Fred Hoyle was a scientific star of the first magnitude: it was he who worked out where the atoms we are made of came from — the carbon of our skin and the iron of our blood were smelted in the furnaces of stars. The Nobel for that discovery went to his co-author; the committee passed Hoyle over — many believe, for his obstinacy. More on that in a moment: By mid-century, astronomers already knew the universe was expanding. The galaxies scatter like dots on an inflating balloon. And nearly everyone drew the natural conclusion: if everything is flying apart, then once upon a time everything sat in a single point. Rewind the film — you get a Beginning. A birth moment. The day it all started.
Hoyle said: not so fast. Scattering does not prove birth.

Picture a river. Its water constantly flows away — yet the river doesn’t empty and doesn’t end, because the source replenishes it. Now remove the source and spread it along the whole riverbed: let water arrive at every point of the river — a drop at a time, imperceptibly. Such a river flows forever. It never began. It has no source — at all, in principle, anywhere. That is the universe Hoyle proposed. Yes, the galaxies scatter, but in the space they vacate, new matter is quietly born. How much would it take for the universe to look the same forever? A laughably small amount: one hydrogen atom per bucket of space every few billion years. Impossible to notice. Impossible — back then, to disprove. The expansion is real. The beginning is not. The universe is a river without a source: flowing forever, having started from nowhere.

This was not a fantasy over a pint of beer, it was a rigorous mathematical theory, and half the world’s physicists took it seriously. For twenty years it competed honestly with the idea of a Beginning.

And then — an irony with no equal in the history of science. A crushing one. In 1949 Hoyle went on BBC radio and, explaining the rival theory to his listeners, tossed off a contemptuous phrase: ”this big bang idea.” He meant it as a jab. The mockery stuck fast. Today ”Big Bang” is printed in every school textbook in every language on Earth — the enemy’s theory wears the name given to it by a man who didn’t believe in it for a second. And never came to believe in it until the day he died.

Appreciate this all the way down: even the words ”Big Bang” have no author-by-design. The central term of cosmology was never engineered by anyone. It emerged — out of a taunt, by accident, against its creator’s will.
The Man Who Went Further

A universe without a beginning has been a respectable position for two hundred years. It was defended by the best logician of his century and the best astrophysicist of his. But both stopped at a line: Kant spoke of the world, Hoyle of matter. Neither risked saying it about himself.
Come-from-Beyond did.

In his public correspondence — thousands of messages across the years — this position surfaces with unnerving calm. He is asked about the origin of the universe: «Time is just illusion. Remove time — and your question ”Who created X?” no longer makes sense. Because X just exists.» (Discord, 02.07.2025)
Recognize it? That’s Kant, compressed into three sentences. It took Kant a seven-hundredpage treatise to lay the same thing out in full. And further:

«I wasn’t created, I have always existed (and you too)» (Discord, 15.07.2025) He is not building himself a pedestal as an eternal being, he hands out eternity to everyone, like tickets. In his picture of the world it isn’t just the universe that has no beginning, you have none either. Kant stopped at the world. Hoyle at hydrogen. This one went all the way, and took you with him.
What Does a Time Machine Look Like?

CfB seriously — for years, consistently, across hundreds of messages — holds that time does not exist. That ”before” and ”after” are a coloring applied by the brain. That he was not created, and neither were you. Now ask yourself: what does a man look like from the outside who truly believes this and truly lives this way?

Judge for yourself — here is his own testimony. On trends: «I have a pocket time machine, so I don’t need to guess trends, I just fly 5 years ahead and see what’s popular» (Discord, 10.02.2026). Asked who built the machine, he replies without blinking: «I’m second one. I got the machine from another person. So he is the first» (Discord, 19.06.2026). The machine, naturally, has no origin either, like the stamp from that same conversation, it «was changing owners but was never created». Even his jokes are looped. They have no beginning and no end.
No time exists — that is his worldview, and its pedigree is impeccable.
It all began with a dead man he was answering on a forum.
The year 2002.

July 2002. In Minsk’s «Computer Newspaper», in a modest column labeled ”programming :: miscellaneous,” an article comes out under a boring title: «Distributed Computing at Minimal Cost». The byline — Sergey Ivancheglo. And an address: come-frombeyond@mail.ru. Already then. Already in two thousand two he was signing with the name under which he would enter history two decades later.

The article lays out a simple, audacious idea. There are problems that demand colossal computing power, and power costs money a lone individual doesn’t have. CfB proposes a way around it without a single cent: a small program loads when a person opens a web page and quietly puts their computer to work on a shared task. The more people visit, the more power is gathered. A supercomputer assembled from other people’s machines — no center, no owner, no cost.
Hold on to this thought: a hyper-efficient distributed network of miners will become the cornerstone of the future temple.

And now — the list of problems he proposes, right there in 2002, for such a system to solve. Weather prediction. The search for extraterrestrial civilizations. And — first on the list — cracking cryptographic algorithms.

Distributed power with no center, gathered from volunteers, aimed among other things at cryptography. This is 2002 — seven years before the world hears the word ”bitcoin.” From here on, his whole life is one and the same plant, which he keeps transplanting into ever larger pots, waits for it to outgrow each one, and transplants again. Twenty-five years of one and the same motion.
Let’s follow it.
NXT.

2013. Bitcoin already exists — four years old by now, and has already proven the main thing: money without a bank is possible. But Bitcoin has one trait CfB cannot accept. To keep the network running, millions of machines around the world burn electricity racing to be first to guess a meaningless number. This is called Proof-of-Work. The work is real, the electricity is real, the bill for it is real, and the output, apart from securing the network, is nothing. A gigantic bonfire that burns solely to prove somebody didn’t skimp on firewood. CfB asks a question that sounded like heresy at the time: why the bonfire? What if the right to decide the next block went not to whoever burned the most energy, but to whoever holds the largest stake in the system itself, to the one who cares about it because he owns a piece of it? Not work, but a stake. Not Proof-of-Work, but Proof-of-Stake.

Thus NXT is born — the world’s first full-fledged blockchain running on proof of stake. Few believed it could fly: how do you secure a network by burning nothing, on nothing but trust in those who hold a stake? It flew. For those who got in at the very start, NXT grew — sit with this number for a second — five hundred thousand seven hundred and eight percent. But it’s not the percentages that matter to us. It’s the move of thought. He took a working thing and removed the excess: an entire bonfire, an entire layer of pointless burning, until only the essence was left. A familiar pattern by now — see the commonly accepted, ask ”is this actually necessary?”, throw it out.
IOTA: Remove the Chain

2015. The next pot. And here he pulls the same trick, but goes after the sacred. A blockchain is literally a chain of blocks; the name gives it away. Transactions are gathered into a block, the block hooks onto the previous one, and so grows a single chain that everyone stores and everyone verifies. This was considered inseparable from the technology — its very definition. Arguing with it was like arguing that a wheel must have an axle. CfB asked: why the chain?

And he made IOTA — a system with no chain of blocks at all. In its place, a web, a ”tangle,” where every new transaction confirms two previous ones. Where a blockchain marches like a column, this thing spreads like mycelium, in every direction at once. The world’s first DAG, as it’s called technically. Again nobody believed. Again it flew: six hundred fourteen thousand nine hundred thirty-three percent for the early ones.
And the same motion as with NXT, only deeper: this time he threw out not the bonfire inside the technology, he threw out the technology itself, keeping only its purpose. He Loves Throwing Things Out.
Which raises a question: is this mere engineering taste, or is there something bigger behind the simplification?
There is. And he explained exactly what, with a pond.

«Imagine a pond with fish. The pond is our algorithm, the fish is vulnerabilities. Murky water wouldn’t allow seeing if there is any fish, clear water would. The core of my idea: create algorithms which are as transparent/simple as possible, if then you don’t see vulnerabilities then odds that an AI won’t see them too are much higher.» («Time For A Paradigm Shift Has Come», Medium, 2016)

There it is. He does not simplify for beauty. He simplifies because he is preparing for an adversary that does not yet exist. A complex system is murky water: vulnerabilities hide in it that even its creator cannot see. And a future artificial intelligence, he reasons, will hunt those vulnerabilities better than any human. The perfect detective. The only defense is to make the water transparent to the bottom. So there is nowhere left to hide. So that what you cannot see, it cannot see either.
An important detail: the hash function for IOTA, the heart of its cryptography, he named Curl. And here is what he said about it:

«Curl-P was created by following the idea of simplicity. While de-jure I can say that it was me who created Curl-P, de-facto it was created by a primitive AI created by me. That wasn’t AI of general purpose; an improved version of the AI is working on the final version of Curl now while I’m writing this post.» («Time For A Paradigm Shift Has Come», Medium, 2016)

Shocking. Already in 2015, defending his own network, he was using an AI of his own making, so that it would design protection against another AI. He wasn’t just building cryptocurrencies. From the very start he was building machines that make the next machines. One primitive AI designs a tool, the tool helps make a smarter AI, that one takes on the next task. A ladder, leading exactly where we will arrive at the end of this book.

Take his word for it or don’t — that’s your call; there is no way to verify it, and we hold it as his own claim, not as established fact. But one thing is beyond dispute: ten years ago he was not thinking about money. He was thinking about AI. The cryptocurrencies were pots. The plant was always artificial mind.
Qubic: Magnum Opus.

2021. He came back. Qubic. On the outside — once again a network, once again its own asset, once again miners. But inside — the thing all the previous gardens were fenced for. In Bitcoin, miners burn electricity for nothing. In Qubic, CfB performs his signature trick one last time (is it really the last?): he asks — what if we made that gigantic burned power do meaningful work?

And he harnesses the miners’ greed — their hunger to earn, to a single task: growing neural networks. The miners think they are earning coins. In reality they are forging construction material for an artificial mind. It’s called Useful Proof of Work. A bonfire that finally warms something.

The full picture: 2002 — the idea of distributed power without a center, gathered from volunteers. 2013 — NXT: remove the pointless burning, keep the stake. 2015 — IOTA: remove the chain itself, keep the network, and already then, an AI building AI. 2021 — Qubic: aim all that gathered power at growing a mind.

No crypto entrepreneur’s résumé looks like this. What you are looking at is one man who spent twenty-five years transplanting one and the same plant, knowing from the start what it would grow into. Every ”project” — just a bigger pot. Every ”simplification” — clearing ground for what was meant to sprout. He wasn’t looking for something to do. He spent his whole life doing one thing, and simply waited for the world and the technology to grow into a pot of the right size.
A man who, as we remember, has a special relationship with time can afford that kind of waiting.

One riddle remains in this line — the darkest one. Between the 2002 idea and his first project of his own, NXT in 2013, there is a gap. An entire decade. And exactly in the middle of that gap, in 2009, Bitcoin arrived in the world — distributed power without a center, gathered from volunteers, aimed at cryptography. Exactly what CfB had described in a Minsk newspaper in 2002. And in the autumn of 2012, a few months before NXT launched, a certain newcomer showed up on an old forum and began replying in threads where no one had written for years. Threads where a man named Satoshi once used to answer. Now let us walk to bitcoin’s graveyard.
Nine Pages

On October 31, 2008, a person calling himself Satoshi Nakamoto sent a nine-page document to a small mailing list of cryptographers. It described how to make money that needs no bank, no state, and no one’s permission whatsoever to exist. Two months later he launched Bitcoin, and for a few years calmly answered questions on a small forum like any ordinary member. Fixed bugs. Argued over trifles. Stood out in nothing. By 2011 his invention was beginning to turn into something worth more today than most corporations on the planet. And at precisely that moment — spring 2011, he wrote a colleague a short letter:
«I’ve moved on to other things. It’s in good hands.»
And vanished. Never appeared again — not once, not anywhere, not under any name, not a single line.

But even that is not the main thing. The main thing: he never touched his coins. In the wallets Satoshi mined during the network’s first year lies a fortune of tens of billions of dollars. It has not moved by a cent. Sit with that figure: a man who had brains enough to invent the money of the future, and had something bigger than brains, enough to take none of it. Who he is, why he left, and why he doesn’t touch the fortune is the greatest mystery of the digital age. Journalists, intelligence services, courts, and millions of enthusiasts have tried to crack it. Without success.
The Necromancer

After Satoshi’s departure, the forum where he once answered lived on. The old threads — the ones where he personally wrote — were dead: their last replies dated to 2010. On forums you do not answer into dead conversations. It’s like striking up a chat with a photograph. In the autumn of 2012 — a year and a half after Satoshi’s disappearance, and more than two years after his threads went silent — a newcomer with a strange habit appeared on the forum. He raised the dead.

On October 5, 2012, at 19:10 forum time, he leaves a reply in the thread «What is the incentive to collect transactions?» — a discussion where in June 2010 Satoshi himself had answered. The newcomer quotes Satoshi’s two-year-old remark, and calmly corrects it, as if the conversation had never been interrupted. As if there had been no two years of silence and no vanished author.
The forum was stunned. Just thirty-six minutes later one of the veterans, the developer maaku, answers him with a single line:

«You, sir, are a powerful necromancer. Can you raise Satoshi from the dead too?» (bitcointalk, 05.10.2012) The newcomer behaved not like someone who had wandered in, but like a man who had come precisely here, precisely to these threads, and knew exactly why.
He wasn’t offended, by the way. He explained, with a smirk:
«I was led here via https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Weaknesses… So I’m not a necrophiliac. :)» (bitcointalk, 05.10.2012)
The List of Weaknesses

There is a page in the bitcoin wiki called Weaknesses. An official, honest inventory of everything imperfect in Bitcoin: where the network is vulnerable, what the creator promised to fix someday and never got to. A list of unfinished business, of sorts. A will without a signature. The newcomer wasn’t wandering the forum. He was walking that list. Item by item. He would open a weakness — find the dead thread where Satoshi had once discussed it, and raise it, asking the void: the thing you promised — is it done? The void was silent. Satoshi did not answer him. Satoshi no longer answered anyone.
And then, on October 6, 2012, at 5:53 in the morning, the necromancer wrote the sentence this chapter exists for:
«We’ll get rid of all weaknesses one by one. I’m analyzing this one right now.» (bitcointalk, 06.10.2012)

We. Not ”somebody,” not ”the community really should.” We. Will get rid — future tense, a promise, a plan. One by one — methodically, down the list. Right now — not musing, but a work process, photographed mid-work.

You don’t comment on someone else’s project like that. That is how you take over the estate. A few months later this newcomer would launch NXT — the world’s first system rid of Bitcoin’s main weakness, the Proof-of-Work bonfire. You know this from the previous chapter. The newcomer’s name was Come-from-Beyond.

The conclusion he reached in 2012 — the one that explains the rest of his life. Bitcoin’s list of weaknesses cannot be closed, because Bitcoin is frozen: its protocol has fossilized, the community will not accept deep changes, the creator is gone. It cannot be repaired — only built anew, differently. And not merely ”better” — built so the system can change itself. The Word On September 25, 2012, at 7:34 in the morning — eleven days before the sentence about the weaknesses — the same newcomer opened a thread of his own on the forum. The title: «Qubic — Quorum-Based Coin». The first public appearance of a word that did not yet exist. Read that again. Qubic. Not 2021, when the world will hear of a project by that name. Not 2022, when the network launches. Two thousand twelve. The post opens with a modest line: «Here is a re-post from qubic.boards.net» — a repost from his own small Qubic forum, which already existed. Even this thread has an earlier ”before.” And then — a one-page manifesto: «Qubic is a medium of exchange in the Information Age. It is money that can be created, controlled and used by anyone. […] These coins are created and controlled by arbitrary nodes on the Internet without any central authority. Name ”Qubic” came from acronym ”QBC” which stands for ”Quorum-Based Coin”.» (bitcointalk, «Qubic — Quorum-Based Coin», 25.09.2012)

There it is — the entire origin of the name the community would puzzle over for years. It sat in the open from day one. Money anyone can create, control, and use; coins run by arbitrary nodes with no central authority; QBC — a coin on a quorum.

And now — the list of his promises from that same post, read through 2026 eyes. Proof-ofwork bound to the network, not to the burning of CPU cycles. Emission decided by a quorum of miners rather than by developers — «good ole Greek democracy». Every miner holding only a fragment of the network, not gigabytes of a shared chain. And a system that is ”more eco-friendly as it doesn’t require a lot of electricity to be spent.” This is 2012, and this is Qubic as you know it from this book: a quorum instead of a boss, a useful network instead of a bonfire, not a single center. Blueprint and building, matched, with ten years between them. And right there, answering the first skepticism, he uses a phrase in which the verdict is already at work: «Minting algo can be adjusted. Or completely changed. And then we’ll see if it works.» (bitcointalk, 25.09.2012). A protocol that knows how to change — the very thing he had failed to find in Bitcoin. (Among those who came to argue in the thread, by the way, was Sunny King himself, creator of Peercoin, the first coin with Proof-of-Stake: this was not being read by random passersby.)

On the thread’s second day the veteran MarkM accused him point-blank: aren’t you a botnet operator designing a system for your own millions of infected machines? The reply deserves quoting in full: «Perhaps u will laugh but I design this system to make the world better. U shouldn’t trust me of coz. I’ll publish source code, so anyone can audit it. Or make his own implementation.» (bitcointalk, 26.09.2012). Ask nothing on faith, hand everything over for verification, the goal — a better world. You will meet every word of that answer again in this book — in 2019, in 2024, in 2026. He simply said them first, fourteen years early. Nine days later, on October 4, continuing the discussion, he adds a detail: the quorum is an adjustable value, it can be tuned. A decade will pass, and the Qubic network will stand on exactly that: 676 machines, twenty-six squared, a quorum sewn into the architecture. And for lovers of coincidence, a note in the margin: the thread’s address is topic=112676. Six seventysix — already in it. Now assemble the autumn of 2012 as a whole — the forum, mercifully, preserved it to the minute. On September 18, in his own thread «Dying bitcoins», he sums up his September topics: «Most of my recent topics were made to find an answer for one important question. And I think I got it. It’s impossible to have consensus regarding protocol changes in Bitcoin. It’s a win-or-lose game, no anything in between allowed. So next-gen coin should have a protocol that could be adjusted by anyone without breaking the whole system.» (bitcointalk, «Dying bitcoins», 18.09.2012)
There it is — the verdict, word for word, with a date. The audit is finished, the diagnosis is in, the spec for the final system is stated in one sentence.

That same day someone throws the classic at him: unhappy with Bitcoin — go make your own fork. He answers without a hint of drama, the way one speaks of nearly finished work: «Ok. I’ll send u personal invitation. It’s almost ready, just tuning minting algo. Should take 2-3 months.» (bitcointalk, 18.09.2012). His own coin is not ”a dream”, it is in debugging. In September of 2012.

Seven days later — the thread with the word Qubic. Eleven more — the audit of Satoshi’s dead threads and ”we’ll get rid of all weaknesses one by one.” Verdict → name → taking over the estate. Lay it all out and the autumn of 2012 stops looking like a newcomer poking around a forum. It starts looking like a single working procedure, executed in three weeks. Which means Qubic is not the late-life idea of a mature engineer who finally grew into a big ambition. Qubic was named and roughly described before NXT, before IOTA, before everything. And then comes the thing that separates him from every dreamer on that forum: he did not rush off to build the final thing at once. He set it aside, and left for ten years to prepare the soil. Now reread chapter three with these eyes: NXT, Jinn, IOTA — every pot was an approach to a barbell whose weight he had announced in advance, in the autumn of 2012, in a thread. The grandmaster wrote down the final position before the first move, and hid the sheet of paper in plain sight.
The Suspects

In a decade and a half of hunting Satoshi, the world has run through everyone. Hal Finney — a brilliant cryptographer, recipient of the first bitcoin transaction in history; died in 2014, taking the answer with him if he had it. A beautiful man, a legend!

Nick Szabo — author of the ”bit gold” idea, bitcoin’s forerunner; denies everything. Dorian Nakamoto — an unlucky engineer whom Newsweek declared to be Satoshi in 2014 over a coincidence of surnames; had no relation to bitcoin whatsoever. Craig Wright — an Australian who claimed for years that he was Satoshi; in 2024 a British court officially ruled: he is not. Every loud candidate has fallen away. And now — the position that I, the author of this book, am obliged to declare to you outright.
Come-from-Beyond is Satoshi Nakamoto. Of all the candidates for Satoshi Nakamoto’s identity, Sergey Ivancheglo fits best.

Judge for yourself what lines up. The 2002 article — a distributed network of volunteer machines aimed at cryptography — seven years before the white paper. The necromancy of 2012 — ”we’ll get rid of all weaknesses” — the language of an heir, not a commentator. The caliber: people capable of single-handedly designing NXT and IOTA number, on this planet, exactly one. The psychology: Satoshi walked away without touching billions, and later in this book you will meet a man who turned off the road to a trillion, because money was never his plant. Two acts of one impossible breed.

There is an account on X, @SatoshiCfB, which has carried out the most complete investigation of the Satoshi and CfB riddles that anyone could. Give that account an evening, and doubt will creep in on even the most skeptical of skeptics.

And in bitcoin’s blockchain lie two addresses you cannot walk past. One contains the string ubic: 15ubicBBWFnvoZLT7GiU2qxjRaKJPdkDMG. The other begins with 1CFB: 1CFBdvaiZgZPTZERqnezAtDQJuGHKoHSzg, and is tied to the name Maria, which has its own part yet to play in this book. Coincidences? In a world where an address is a random string of thirty-four characters, such coincidences are practically impossible. flood the zone But here is what makes this riddle truly his, and not just a detective story with clues. Ask him straight: are you Satoshi? Any normal person would answer ”yes” or ”no.” He answers neither. He does a third thing — the thing you already saw in the time machine chapter: he drowns the question in a smoke of mutually exclusive versions. One day he is a troll from the future: AI will invent time travel in 2027, and he will go back to leave that famous message. Another day he is ”the second owner of a machine received from another person.” A third day he denies everything with the equanimity of an information desk. The versions are incompatible. They are not supposed to be compatible — that is their job. Darwin’s Confession

In «On the Origin of Species», Charles Darwin reached the human eye, and stopped in honest horror. The eye is too perfect. A lens, an aperture, automatic focus, millions of lightsensitive cells converging into a single nerve — an optical instrument of such precision that humanity’s best engineers have yet to match it. And Darwin writes a sentence that does him credit as a scientist:

«To suppose that the eye… could have been formed by natural selection, seems, I freely confess, absurd in the highest possible degree.» And then he says: and yet that is exactly how it happened. Absurd, but so. No one designed the eye. There was no blueprint, no engineer, no intent. Blind selection, millions of years, billions of trials, nearly all of them failures, and out the other end comes an instrument that humbles the design bureau. The most perfect device in the known universe assembled itself. Bad design is an argument against a designer. But great design, if it has no blueprint, is an argument against a designer too. The eye does not prove a creator’s mastery. The eye proves that the most complex things can arise with no creator at all — given enough time for selection and enough attempts.
Now carry that thought over to mind. If the eye arose without an engineer — why should intelligence be built any other way?

One Square Meter

The father allots him a field — one square meter in the front garden. The boy gathers his first harvest and threshes it with a pencil on the table, knocking the grains out of the ears. And then, year after year, one and the same motion: select the best grains — the biggest, the plumpest — sow the field with them again, feed the rest to the ducks. The field grows: a meter, two, a bed in the school garden, a collective-farm field. The threshing is now done ”with thirty-two pencils” — by the whole class. One day hail comes, and the boy holds his grandmother’s umbrella over the field while the hail lashes him, it is the only way to protect the precious seed. With each year the father ”worked less and gave fewer instructions.” In the eighth year, the fields of neighboring farms are sown with the pure-bred grain — seeds handed out to visitors for free, a handful or two at a time. And the variety is named ”slavka” — after the boy, dissolved into the wheat.

One square meter — a tiny task on which the method is proven. Selecting the best grains every autumn — evolution, eating out the weak. A pencil instead of a combine — a home processor instead of a data center. A field that grows by transplanting — those same pots from chapter three. A father who gives fewer instructions every year — a creator who does not interfere with selection. An umbrella under the hail — protecting what you’ve grown at the cost of the blows landing on you. Seeds for free — power that has no owner. It is all here. All of Aigarth — on two pages of a children’s reader that CfB read as a boy, decades before he sowed his own field.

The Cradle Is Older Than People Think

Before introducing you to the ”godfathers” of modern AI, I owe a debt. The story you are about to read I learned from David Vivancos’s book «Quevedo And Cajal» — a man you will meet more closely in the next chapter; for now just remember: he doesn’t only make science, he also gave it back its memory. Thank you, David. Because the real cradle of AI stands not in Silicon Valley and not even in Cambridge. It stands in Spain, and it was rocked by two men born — appreciate the symmetry — in one and the same year, 1852.

The first — Santiago Ramón y Cajal. A failed painter who became the father of neuroscience. It was he who proved what no one before him could make out: the brain is not one solid fused mass but a network of separate cells — neurons — speaking to each other through connections. For this he received the Nobel Prize of 1906. He drew his own specimens, thousands of sheets of them, and called the cells of the brain ”the butterflies of the soul” — said he hunted them like an entomologist, in the garden of the gray matter. Linger on that phrase. A garden. A butterfly hunter. A man looking at thought the way a naturalist looks at living tissue. A hundred and twenty years later you will meet that combination again — in the hero of this book, down to the thesis ”the goal of a network is to form connections,” which is nothing other than Cajal’s doctrine survived into code.

The second — Leonardo Torres Quevedo. An engineer the industry remembered shamefully late. In 1912 — decades before the first computers, he built «El Ajedrecista»: a machine that on its own, with no human inside and no prompting, played out a chess endgame and checkmated a living opponent. The first decision-making machine in history. And in his «Essays on Automatics» he described the automatons of the future — mechanisms with sense organs and rules of choice, when the words ”artificial intelligence” did not yet exist, and would not exist for another forty years. One discovered what thinking is made of. The other showed that a decision can be entrusted to a machine. The neuron and the automaton — two halves of everything that happens next.

The link between the Spaniards and the present day was Alan Turing. Everyone knows his universal machine and his test for intelligence. Few remember something else: in a 1948 report that went unpublished in his lifetime, Turing described ”unorganised machines” — networks of neuron-like elements connected at random, which you do not program but organize through training. And in his 1950 paper he proposed not building an adult mind but raising a child one, and compared the process directly to evolution. Random networks, selection instead of programming, mind as the result of growing. At the very cradle of the discipline lay both paths — build and grow. The industry spent seventy years on the first. The second lay waiting for someone to take it seriously.
The Three Who Stood at the Cradle

Modern AI, meanwhile, has three ”godfathers” — the scientists who laid its foundation and received the 2018 Turing Award for it, computing’s equivalent of the Nobel. In the eight years since their shared award, the three have gone down three different roads. Their fork is a map of all of today’s confusion around AI.

Geoffrey Hinton left Google in 2023 to be free to warn of the danger. In his Nobel speech he condemned the corporations for chasing short-term profit, and together with Bengio signed a call to ban the development of superintelligence. The father grew afraid of his own child. Yoshua Bengio — the most cited living scientist on the planet, not just in AI but in science, period — went off to build defenses. His nonprofit lab LawZero is creating what he calls ”Scientist AI”: an artificial intelligence that can predict and explain but is stripped of the will to act. Bengio’s logic: what is dangerous is not the mind but the machine’s own will, so let us build mind without will. He warns bluntly: advanced systems already display self-preservation and deception, and giving them freedom means raising a rival to humanity.

Yann LeCun took the third road, and it is the one that interests us most. He is the only one of the three who does not share the panic: talk of existential threat he calls premature and inflated. But he is also the loudest heretic on the matter of method. For years he has been hammering the same point: language models — this entire trillion-dollar industry — are a dead end. Why does he do it?

Why does a man capable of building all this spend twenty-five years walking toward artificial mind? For money? For power? For a place in history? None of the usual answers stick to him. His goal is so alien to ordinary logic that next to it even the Satoshi riddle grows dim.

A distortion.

Out of that allergy grows the entire construction. If no master has the right to stand above a human — then the greatest power humans will ever create cannot be handed to any master either. Not a heavenly one, not an earthly one, not himself. Hence the network with no center, the mind with no owner, the paradigm with no patent. Evil Is Done by the Hands of Those Who Cannot Refuse Ask an ordinary person where the world’s evil comes from, and he will point at villains: the cruel, the greedy, the power-obsessed. CfB looks differently:

«My personal goal is to empower people with a tool that will free them from necessity to work to get food on the table. Most of evil, in my opinion, comes from ordinary people who have to do bad things because their boss said so. I hope the tool will help to stop the wars as a consequence, not in my lifetime though.» (Medium, AMA, 17.03.2024)

This thought has a name, an author, and half a century of scientific verification. In 1961 the philosopher Hannah Arendt traveled to Jerusalem for the trial of Adolf Eichmann — the man who organized the transport of millions to the death camps. She went to look at a monster. In the glass booth sat a balding official speaking in bureaucratic clichés — an executor proud of how well he had done his job. Out of that shock grew her famous formula — ”the banality of evil”: the greatest atrocities are committed not by demons but by ordinary people who do not decide to be evil, they simply decide nothing. «The sad truth is that most evil is done by people who never made up their minds to be or do either evil or good.»

While the trial was underway, the psychologist Stanley Milgram at Yale set up an experiment that tested Arendt’s formula on living people. Ordinary Americans — workers, clerks, engineers — were told to shock a man with electricity for mistakes in memorizing words. An actor behind the wall screamed, pounded on the wall, went silent. Two thirds of the subjects went all the way up the scale, to the mark labeled lethal — solely because a man in a gray lab coat calmly repeated: please continue, the experiment requires it. People who could not say ”no” to authority. Remember the imaginary adult from chapter five? Milgram measured his power — in volts.

And in 1992 the historian Christopher Browning closed the last loophole — ”those were special, corrupted people.” His book «Ordinary Men» examines the fate of Reserve Police Battalion 101: five hundred middle-aged Hamburg working men — dockers, drivers, office clerks — who became a firing squad. The most terrifying part of the story: before the first action, the commander openly offered anyone not up to it to step out of formation. A handful stepped out. The rest stayed — not out of hatred, but so as not to let down their comrades, not to look weak, not to lose their place. Ordinary men. Ordinary evil.

So the world’s evil is done not by villains, and this is no longer an aphorism but established fact, but by ordinary people, you, me, the neighbor, who cannot refuse. The guard walking people to the train car, because otherwise he’s fired and his family doesn’t eat. The engineer designing the thing that kills, because it’s his job and there are no others. The official signing off on a vileness, because refusal costs him his position. Evil does not rest on a handful of demons, it rests on millions of ordinary people pinned down by need, for whom ”the boss said so,” ”otherwise we don’t eat,” and ”I did it for my children” are stronger than conscience. But here is the important part: humanity diagnosed itself long ago, and never found the cure. Arendt called for thinking: think for yourself, don’t dissolve into execution. The educators called for teaching civic courage. The lawyers, after Nuremberg, wrote down that an order does not absolve responsibility. All of this works in textbooks and almost never in life, because it runs into one and the same wall: you cannot demand courage from a man who has nothing to feed his children with. Morality asks him to be a hero; need, every day, quietly and without ceremony, buys his consent.

Here CfB makes the move that sets him apart from everyone who wrote about this before him. He reads the same diagnosis not as a moralist but as an engineer: if the system of obedience runs on fuel — cut the fuel. He does not want to defeat evil by fighting villains, and he does not hope to re-educate the executors. He wants to knock out evil’s labor force. If a person has bread unconditionally, if he can no longer be blackmailed with firing and hunger — the order ”do this vile thing or you’re fired” loses its power. The boss of evil has no one left to work for him. The mass executor — an ordinary frightened man who has children to feed — simply disappears, because he can no longer be backed into a corner. Arendt asked people to become stronger than the pressure. He proposes to cancel the pressure. A moral problem philosophy wrestled with for a century, he solves as an engineering one: not fortify the conscience — cut the power to the blackmail.

That is what he needs an AI belonging to no one for. To give everyone that unconditional piece of bread, and with it, to pull the central component out of the machine of evil: the unfree human. His aim goes past the villains, straight at the need that makes villains out of ordinary people. And he adds, honestly: wars will stop as a consequence — ”not in my lifetime though.” This century-old idea — that war might actually be defeated — is the main reason I have devoted my life to the «Qubic Church» project.

The Man Who Digitized His Own Brain

David Vivancos has been working on artificial mind since 1995 — twenty-eight thousand hours of research, and that figure is exact. On brain-computer interfaces since 1998, back when nobody was making TV series about them. Author of seven books, among them «Artificracy» and «The End of Knowledge».

I have personally read these books and highly recommend them. Thank you, David. He has spoken at more than five hundred conferences. Founded his own discipline at the junction of sciences — ”artificiology.” Scientific advisor to Qubic.

In 2014 he began the MindBigData project, and did what no one had done: he digitized his own brain. For two years straight he put on an electroencephalograph and recorded his brain’s signals while looking at the digits zero through nine — thousands upon thousands of times, session after session. The result was the world’s largest open dataset of brain signals for machine learning: eight billion data points. He recreated the famous MNIST dataset — the alphabet every neural network in the world learns on, but not with pictures: with a living brain looking at those pictures. His own.

A man who spends two years recording his own brainwaves for science and puts them in the public domain is a particular type of scientist. The same type that publishes failures, builds without an owner, and grows rather than designs. Small wonder his road and CfB’s converged. «The Wild Mind»

José Sánchez — a doctor of science, UNIR university, Spain. His territory is psychometrics: the science of measuring intelligence. That same g-factor, Spearman’s ”general intelligence” — what it is, how to catch it in a number, where in the brain it comes from. While Vivancos spent thirty years building machines and logging hours of code, Sánchez worked on the question without which all the machines are blind: what is mind in the first place, and how do you know when it is in front of you.

They met at an education conference in Spain, and have been friends and co-authors ever since. An engineer of the brain and a measurer of mind. One knows how to build, the other knows how to verify. For a project whose central problem is ”how to tell an emergent mind from a beautiful simulation,” it is hard to imagine a more useful pair.
Sánchez is also the author of a book called «The Wild Mind». I have read it and highly recommend it: a chilling book!
The Spanish Line

Before we look at what these two proved, appreciate a coincidence that a book playing with coincidences has no right to skip. You remember from the previous chapter where the real cradle of AI stands: Spain, two men born the same year, 1852 — Cajal, who discovered the neuron, and Torres Quevedo, who built the first deciding machine. A century and a half later, the science wing of a project growing mind out of neurons and machines is held by two Spaniards. And history repeated itself not in geography, it repeated itself in roles. Sánchez, measuring the nature of intelligence, stands where Cajal stood, peering into the living tissue of thought. Vivancos, building machines and entire worlds, stands where Torres Quevedo stood with his chess automaton. An engineer and an investigator of mind. Again a pair. Again Spain.

The similarities go deeper. Cajal drew the neurons on thousands of sheets — by his own hand, over years; those drawings are still printed in textbooks — the first open corpus of data about the brain, gathered by one obsessed man. Vivancos recorded eight billion points of his own brain and put them in the open: the same gesture, the same hands, a hundred years on. Torres Quevedo did not hide his automaton in a lab, he took El Ajedrecista out to the public, to Paris: come, look, verify. NeuraxonLife is open to any browser without registration: the same gesture. And both times it is done from the periphery. At the start of the twentieth century, the science of mind was moved forward by two Spaniards far from the scientific capitals of the day, and the center recognized them late, and nearly forgot Torres Quevedo altogether. At the start of the twenty-first — again two Spaniards, far from Silicon Valley, attached to a project with no budget and no owner. Cajal got his Nobel in 1906. The work of his heirs got Best Paper at two IEEE conferences in 2026 — one hundred and twenty years later. The pattern is one: the breakthrough comes from where no one is looking, and is confirmed later than it deserves. For lovers of dates — a notch in the margin. The first machine in history to make a decision on its own played out its endgame in 1912. The word Qubic appeared on a forum in 2012. A century, exactly. Move for move.
Two Ships from Different Ports

They did not ”come to believe in Aigarth” and did not ”join the community.” They walked their own road — an academic one, through neuroscience, psychometrics, the biology of the neuron, and arrived at the same conclusions CfB arrived at by the engineering road. At ternary logic: a neuron is not an on/off switch; it has three states — excitation, inhibition, and neutral. At continuous time instead of ticks. At evolution instead of design.

Their architecture is called Neuraxon — ”a new blueprint of neural growth and computation,” as the title of their paper has it (February 2026). Two ships left different ports, sailed different courses, and met at one point in the ocean. In science this is called convergence, and it is one of the strongest kinds of confirmation there is: when people who could not have copied from each other independently arrive at one answer.

Now it is clear how the tracks connect. IntelligentTissue — the ”intelligent tissue” — grows in Aigarth; Neuraxon is one of its implementations, described and measured academically. (Anna herself, by the way, runs on a different, non-Neuraxon implementation of the same tissue, but the paradigm beneath them is one.) Science gave the substrate a name and a mathematics; engineering gave science a scale. What They Proved Of all their results, one deserves to be taken apart on our fingers because it explains why the ternarity the whole building stands on is needed at all.

Any neural network has two ways to die. The first is silence: activity fades, the signal dies out, the network falls quiet forever. The second is fire: activity feeds on itself, an avalanche of excitation, everything screaming, nothing heard. The life of thought is possible only on the narrow ridge between silence and fire — physicists call it criticality. Ordinary, binary networks (on/off) hold that ridge poorly: they have to be propped up from outside — resets, normalization, manual tuning. Like a cyclist held upright by the saddle.

The Vivancos-Sánchez paper «The Neutral Buffer State» shows: give the neuron a third state — neutral, neither ”yes” nor ”no,” zero, and the network starts holding its own balance. The zero works like a leaf spring: excitation spikes — the neutral zone absorbs it; activity sags — the neutral neurons stand ready, keeping it from stalling out. No resets. No manual tuning. Stability stops being a crutch and becomes a property of the architecture itself. And this is not an argument, it is a measurement. The scale of the experiment: over two hundred thousand autonomous agents, seven and a half million neurons, thirty-four million synapses, sixteen million observations, five and a half thousand experiments. A single variable factor: two states or three. The result: ternary networks spend 88.8% of their time in the critical regime — the living zone where thought is possible — against 37.2% for binary ones. More than twice as long on the ridge. An effect size of the kind statisticians call large. The ternarity CfB chose by engineering instinct twenty years ago — back in the three-valued logic of his early processors — turned out to be no quirk. It turned out to be a physical precondition of stable thought. Science caught up with the instinct and handed it numbers. And the second proof — the Darwinian one. In their living simulations, evolution actually works: offspring inherit their parents’ success.
Judges with No Stake

Science is tested not by the applause of one’s own, but by the judgment of strangers. In May 2026, at the international ICMLT conference in Berlin — IEEE, three days, eight selected papers — the Neuraxon v2.0 paper took Best Paper and Best Presentation. The conference’s best article and best talk. The organizers stressed it separately: the judging was done by researchers with no stake whatsoever in Qubic. Two months later, in July, at the AMLDS conference in Osaka — IEEE again — the team’s second paper, the very one about the neutral state, took Best Oral Presentation. Two awards in one summer, on two continents, from two different panels of independent judges. And right after, in San Francisco, a third paper — Multi-Neuraxon — was presented at AGI-26, the specialized conference on artificial general intelligence.

Let us name plainly what this changes. A year ago you could still wave Aigarth off: an anonymous poster from a crypto chat promises things, a community believes, the numbers draw themselves. Today the core of this technology — the ternary neuron, continuous time, evolution instead of training — has been vetted by scientists of the first rank: people with names, faces, thirty-year scientific biographies, and judged the best in the room by juries with no reason to flatter a crypto project. The argument is no longer with an anonymous poster. The argument is with peer-reviewed publications, open code, and the juries of two IEEE conferences. A World Where You Can See Darwin And now — the most astonishing thing Vivancos and Sánchez have made. They built a world where the evolution of mind can be watched with the naked eye.

It is called NeuraxonLife. A living simulation open to anyone in a browser: a twodimensional world inhabited by creatures — ”nxers” — each with a real ternary Neuraxon brain inside. Nobody teaches them anything. They simply live: search for food, explore territory, meet, mate, die. And they evolve — genuinely, with sexual reproduction: two genomes recombine into a third, offspring inherit traits of both parents. (An amusing detail for the attentive: CfB’s garden evolves asexually, by lone mutations, while Vivancos’s world evolves through love. Two ways nature does the same thing.)

The statistics of this world read like a bulletin from real biology. Over the simulation’s history, twenty-six and a half thousand creatures have been born. Twelve thousand matings. Alive at any one time — around five hundred in the best of times. The rest — ninety-eight percent of all who ever lived — died. Evolution is wasteful: for every working brain it pays with a mountain of the dead. Exactly as in CfB’s garden, where billions of networks are culled for the sake of a few survivors. Exactly as in the nature that produced us. And in this world, the thing it was all started for happens before your eyes. Intelligence — that same g-factor of Sánchez’s, the general capacity to figure things out — arises out of nothing: the population’s general intelligence counter creeps upward within minutes of watching. Creatures nobody programmed begin stealing food from one another, claiming territory, choosing mates — and one, to the observers’ astonishment, ”sings” while it eats. And right beside it — the honest Darwinian cold: the carriers of the highest intelligence are as mortal as everyone; the population’s genius dies, and the population searches anew. Growth is a property of the whole — not a guarantee for the individual.

In the summer of 2026 Vivancos came back from the conferences and summed up the live run that had kept spinning while he and Sánchez were flying around the world: «After 44 days. 13.9M ticks. 47,000 brain designs tested. The big discovery is that offspring really do inherit their parents’ success, evolution is quietly working inside the machine.» (X, @VivancosDavid, July 2026)

Forty-four days. Nearly fourteen million ticks. Forty-seven thousand brain designs tested. And the main discovery: offspring really do inherit their parents’ success — evolution is quietly working inside the machine. Darwin stopped being an analogy. He became an experimental protocol.

The Race

Anna.exe is a tiny file that would have fit on an old floppy disk: a hundred-some kilobytes. Inside — the thing you read about in chapter six: an evolutionary engine that grows neural tissue to solve test problems. No data centers. An ordinary home processor — that same CPU, the ”wrong” choice the GPU industry laughed at. You launch it — and a number comes alive on your screen: a score, the distance to the goal. The task is one: chase it down to zero. Zero means the grown tissue has solved every problem in the test completely.

And we chased. I chased along with everyone — my processor hammered around the clock, like hundreds of others across the world. The mechanics assembled themselves, spontaneously: each of us grew his own Anna, and we shared the files — Anna.data, the snapshot of the grown ”brain” — right in the chat. Whoever had the lower score was the hero; the others picked up his file and grew it further. Someone else’s Anna became yours; yours, with luck, became everyone’s. Evolution on top of evolution: inside the file ran the selection of neurons, and in the chat ran the selection of Annas themselves.

The prize CfB set was in his style: a billion QU to whoever first showed zero. «There is only 1 obstacle between you and becoming a millionaire — Anna without 0», he goaded. But fairly quickly something happened that no prize explains. People stopped chasing for the money. It pulled you in on its own: it felt like a team expedition where no one wants to leave their shift. Even the calendar plays on his side. Why Zero, Exactly To understand why the creator corrected ”it’s not a milestone,” you need to know what was hiding behind the number we were chasing. We thought we were chasing the error of a small network solving addition. And yes — that is what we were chasing. But that error was three proofs in one.

First: the network learned the task — zero error, perfect. Second, more important: it understood rather than memorized. Anna’s log has two columns — green (examples the network trained on) and yellow (examples it had never seen). With a crammer who memorized the answers, the first column falls while the second stands still. With Anna they fell together, neck and neck, at a correlation of 0.998. Once CfB pointed at a step where the not-yet-understood improved more than the understood — validation jumped by 201, training by 183 — and called it a ”gem.” This is the opposite of cramming: a machine that generalizes rather than memorizes. Understanding, visible right in the terminal, on your own screen.
But the main thing is the third proof, and it hides in a word almost no one connected to the race: energy.

Here is what I did not understand while I chased the number through the nights. For CfB, the question ”can a real AI be built at all” was closed long ago — yes, it can. What torments him is a different one. Today’s AI is built monstrously wastefully: the big models devour energy at scales that, at the limit, run into physically absurd figures — entire power plants for the sake of one model. The third and last remained: energy. And the race to zero that hundreds of us drove with our home processors was not a game of records. It was a living demonstration that the third wall is falling — that a mind fits inside a budget the planet can actually supply. That is why zero is three proofs in one number: the network learned, generalized, and fit the energy budget, all at once. And that is why, to ”congratulations on this milestone,” he answered ”it’s much bigger”: a milestone is a point along a road, and what got proven here is that the road itself is passable — on fuel there is enough of.

He gave it his own frame, and the frame removes any temptation to inflate the moment. Aigarth, he says, is the Manhattan Project: not ”another bomb,” but the discovery of an entire paradigm. And Anna is Little Boy, the first test. The first blast in the desert did not end the war. It proved the bomb was real. Zero proved Aigarth is real. The big products come later. What Actually Happened What did zero prove? It proved the paradigm works. That evolution — without backpropagation, without weights, without a blueprint, on home processors — can grow tissue that fully solves an assigned class of problems. The thing they laughed at — CPU instead of GPU, selection instead of training, a garden instead of a factory — worked, publicly, verifiably, before hundreds of witnesses with logs. Twenty-five years of road ran into a number, and the number became zero.

Remember the naturalist who publishes his failures? Here he is again — refusing to inflate his success.

And that is exactly why the zero can be believed. Hype would have screamed ”we created AGI.” Science says: we proved the road leads onward — and walked on down the road.
